operations.source_excerpt: 1.2 The function $f(x)=-x$ is 1-Lipschitz and satisfies $f(0)=0$. By [F3] and [F4], its integrals against $\delta_0$ and $\delta_1$ are $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=-1$, so its objective is $1$. Every feasible $g$ has objective $g(0)-g(1)\le|g(0)-g(1)|\le1$, so the dual supremum is exactly $1$. [given, F3, F4, algebra]
operations.proposed_replacement: 1.2 Let $h$ be any feasible real-valued function, so it is 1-Lipschitz and hence continuous and Borel measurable. Its parts $h^+=\max\{h,0\}$ and $h^-=\max\{-h,0\}$ are nonnegative measurable functions by [F4]. Applying [F3] to each part, for $c\in\{0,1\}$ we get $\int h^+\,d\delta_c=h^+(c)<\infty$ and $\int h^-\,d\delta_c=h^-(c)<\infty$. Thus [F4] makes $h$ integrable against both endpoint masses and gives $\int h\,d\delta_c=h^+(c)-h^-(c)=h(c)$. In particular, $f(x)=-x$ is feasible and has integrals $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=-1$, so its objective is $1$. Every feasible $g$ has objective $g(0)-g(1)\le|g(0)-g(1)|\le1$, so the dual supremum is exactly $1$. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

operations.source_excerpt: 1.2 Every function on the finite discrete set is Borel and simple. By [F4], its integrals against $\mu$ and $\nu$ are the corresponding two-point sums, so the objective for a feasible $f$ with $f(a)=0$ is $(p-q)(f(a)-f(b))$. Since $|f(a)-f(b)|\le D$, the objective is at most $D|p-q|$. If $p\ge q$, choose $f(b)=-D$; if $p<q$, choose $f(b)=D$. Each choice is feasible and attains $D|p-q|$, including $p=q$. [given, F1, F4, algebra, choose]
operations.proposed_replacement: 1.2 Every real-valued function $f$ on the finite discrete set is Borel measurable, and $f^+$ and $f^-$ are nonnegative simple functions. For either $\lambda=\mu$ or $\lambda=\nu$, apply the nonnegative finite-sum formula [F4] separately to $f^+$ and $f^-$ to get $\int f^\pm\,d\lambda=f^\pm(a)\lambda(\{a\})+f^\pm(b)\lambda(\{b\})<\infty$. Subtracting these two finite quantities by the signed-integral definition in [F4] proves $\int f\,d\lambda=f(a)\lambda(\{a\})+f(b)\lambda(\{b\})$. Using the atom masses [F2], the objective for a feasible $f$ with $f(a)=0$ is therefore $(p-q)(f(a)-f(b))$. Since $|f(a)-f(b)|\le D$, the objective is at most $D|p-q|$. If $p\ge q$, choose $f(b)=-D$; if $p<q$, choose $f(b)=D$. Each choice is feasible and attains $D|p-q|$, including $p=q$. [given, F1, F2, F4, algebra, choose]
